paras: The attempted lynching of Wash Attaway took place at the jail in Sulphur Springs, Texas, in July 1888, when a mob demanded Attaway, a Black man held for the killing of a white man named Marion Gamblin near Carroll's Prairie. The mob, put at ninety-five men, was kept at bay, and Attaway was later reported released on bail. Texas papers noted the case for its toll: besides Gamblin, two women's deaths were attributed to the affair.

On July 16, 1888, Sheriff Ferguson of Sulphur Springs received a telegram from Carroll's Prairie reporting that Gamblin had been killed and asking for bloodhounds, which he sent at once. According to the Sulphur Springs dispatch, Gamblin had sold Attaway a mule on credit, and when Attaway's security would no longer stand good, Gamblin went to take the animal back. The dispatch said Attaway blocked the yard with a pole, struck Gamblin down, and kept the witness Belton Wilson away, and that neighbors found Gamblin dead with head and arm wounds and a knife wound in his back.

Late that afternoon Attaway rode into Sulphur Springs, reportedly to complain of Gamblin's trespass on his brother's advice, and was heard telling how he had knocked Gamblin down with a club. The sheriff took him to jail, and the same report said that the citizens of Carroll's Prairie were "very indignant" and that Attaway "would have probably died" had he been found there.

Within the next few days a mob surrounded the jail and demanded the prisoner. The Waco evening news reported that ninety-five men "attempted to force the jail but were kept at bay", while the San Antonio daily light said they were "finally dissuaded"; neither named who turned them back.

The Waco evening news reported that Attaway was granted bail of six thousand dollars and that fear of another attack had turned the jail into "a fortress". The same paper said Gamblin's wife, "being in a delicate condition", had died, and that the sheriff's wife, near childbirth, died from the excitement of the threatened attack. No report of an indictment or trial of Attaway, or of action against the mob, appears in the coverage.

The episode survives in four short items from two Texas papers, dated July 17 to July 20. The Waco evening news gave the fullest account under the headline "White Man Murdered", calling Gamblin "very highly esteemed" and Attaway "a negro", and drawing its narrative of the quarrel from the local side. Its follow-up mourned "three estimable people" and reported the mob's attempt without comment for or against it.
The San Antonio daily light carried the killing and the mob as single lines in its "State News" column, saying only that Attaway "narrowly escapes lynching".

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Wash Attaway
bases: A mob surrounded or tried to force the Sulphur Springs jail and demanded the prisoner Wash Attaway, who 'narrowly escapes lynching' (A3, A4).
A mob of ninety-five men sought to take Attaway from jail over the killing of Gamblin, but it was kept at bay or dissuaded and he was not killed (A3, A4); this was an attempted lynching.
Two papers with differently worded and independently detailed reports (Waco evening news and San Antonio daily light) agree that a mob gathered at the jail for Attaway and was turned back (A3, A4).

accounts.label: Sulphur Springs dispatch
accounts.gist: Gamblin came to repossess a mule sold to Attaway on credit; Attaway blocked him with a pole, struck him down, and Gamblin was found dead with head, arm and knife wounds; Attaway then came to town to complain of trespass and was jailed.

accounts.label: Attaway's reported statement
accounts.gist: Attaway was said to have told in town how he knocked Gamblin down with a club, and to have come to make a complaint against Gamblin for trespassing.

accounts.label: Texas state-news reports
accounts.gist: A mob of ninety-five men surrounded or tried to force the jail and demanded Attaway but was kept at bay or dissuaded.

framing.detail: The Waco evening news ran the killing under 'White Man Murdered', praised Gamblin as 'very highly esteemed', and noted that Attaway would 'probably' have died had he been found in the neighborhood, without comment on the threat.
Its follow-up mourned 'three estimable people' and reported the mob's attempt and the jail's defense without condemning or endorsing the mob.
The San Antonio daily light gave the affair one line in its 'State News' column: Attaway 'narrowly escapes lynching'.
